set.stem: A 20-year-old student sees his GP with blurred vision; a year ago he had a dislocated lens. On examination he has pectus excavatum, a high-arched palate and joint hypermobility. Which cardiac disorder is often associated with his condition?
set.explanation: Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), pectus excavatum, a high-arched palate and hypermobility suggest Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 mutation). Mitral valve prolapse is common in Marfan syndrome, while the most dangerous lesion is aortic root dilatation with aortic regurgitation and dissection, monitored by regular imaging and treated with beta-blockers or angiotensin receptor blockers and prophylactic root surgery. Coarctation is associated with Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve, Ebstein anomaly with maternal lithium exposure, and VSD and aortic stenosis are not features of Marfan syndrome.

why: Same idea as valv-0043 (older patient with exertional angina, dizziness/syncope and dyspnoea, a systolic murmur and LVH = aortic stenosis); its ECG description was also garbled
Same idea as valv-0027 (echocardiography is the investigation of choice for a suspected valve lesion); its options also listed colour Doppler separately from echocardiography

set.stem: A patient admitted with pneumonia is found to have a heart murmur. Which finding points to mitral regurgitation?
set.explanation: Mitral murmurs are loudest at the apex and are accentuated by rolling the patient into the left lateral position, which brings the LV apex closer to the chest wall; the MR murmur is pansystolic, radiates to the axilla and is louder in expiration. A murmur louder on inspiration suggests a right-sided lesion, maximal intensity in the right second intercostal space suggests aortic stenosis, Corrigan sign indicates aortic regurgitation, and a narrow pulse pressure is typical of severe aortic stenosis.

why: Same idea as valv-0006 (early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a wide pulse pressure = aortic regurgitation)

set.stem: A 59-year-old man attends for a routine check-up. He is asymptomatic, and examination reveals a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: A mid-systolic click (sudden tensing of the prolapsing leaflet and chordae) followed by a late systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation is mitral valve prolapse, called Barlow syndrome when due to myxomatous degeneration; standing or Valsalva brings the click earlier and lengthens the murmur, and squatting delays them. The Austin Flint murmur is an apical mid-diastolic murmur in severe AR, the Graham Steell murmur an early diastolic murmur of pulmonary regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension, the Carey Coombs murmur a mid-diastolic murmur of acute rheumatic carditis, and a PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur.

set.stem: A 57-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever and essential hypertension presents with worsening breathlessness and reduced exercise tolerance. Which of the following is NOT a clinical sign of mitral stenosis?
set.explanation: Mitral stenosis produces a malar flush (low cardiac output with peripheral vasoconstriction), AF (left atrial dilatation), a tapping undisplaced apex (palpable loud S1) and, once pulmonary hypertension develops, a right ventricular heave. A pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla indicates mitral regurgitation – it may coexist in mixed rheumatic disease but is not a sign of mitral stenosis, whose murmur is an apical mid-diastolic rumble.

set.stem: An asymptomatic 31-year-old woman is told she has mitral valve prolapse after an echocardiogram. Which statement is correct?
set.explanation: Mitral valve prolapse is defined echocardiographically as systolic displacement of one or both mitral leaflets more than 2 mm beyond the annular plane into the left atrium. Most people with MVP are asymptomatic and need no drugs or exercise restriction; beta-blockers are used only for troublesome palpitations, and ACE inhibitors have no role. Only a minority progress to significant MR, mainly those with thickened myxomatous leaflets, so periodic echocardiographic follow-up is advised.

why: MVP is diagnosed by echocardiography, not ECG (stem corrected)
Same idea as valv-0043 (syncope, angina and exertional dyspnoea in an older patient = aortic stenosis with an ejection systolic murmur at the right sternal edge)
Same idea as hf-0058 (dynamic HCM murmur: louder with Valsalva/standing, softer with squatting/handgrip); the source key here (MVP click) was also wrong for this HCM vignette
The same PreTest question as valv-0043, reprinted in another source

set.stem: A 78-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of productive cough, leg swelling and fatigue; he has been afebrile throughout. He had a porcine (bioprosthetic) mitral valve replacement for severe mitral regurgitation 12 years ago. Examination shows bibasal crackles, a laterally displaced apex beat and a grade 3/6 low-pitched diastolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options: Structural degeneration of the bioprosthetic valve
set.explanation: Bioprosthetic (porcine) valves undergo structural deterioration – calcification, leaflet stiffening and tears – with a rising failure rate after about 10 years, earlier in the mitral than the aortic position. A new apical diastolic murmur indicates prosthetic mitral stenosis, and with the heart-failure picture this points to valve degeneration; echocardiography (TTE and TOE) confirms it, and treatment is redo surgery or transcatheter valve-in-valve implantation. Infective endocarditis must always be excluded with blood cultures, but he has been afebrile for 3 weeks, and COPD, pneumonia and PE do not explain a new diastolic murmur.

why: Added 'afebrile' to separate degeneration from endocarditis; abbreviated options written out
Same idea as valv-0043 (elderly patient with progressive symptoms and signs of aortic stenosis); the source stem was underspecified (weak pulses alone)
Same idea as valv-0004 (left heart failure due to mitral regurgitation); the source stem omitted the auscultatory findings needed to answer it

set.stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. He is now alert and, in retrospect, describes occasional substernal chest pressure and breathlessness on exertion. His BP is 110/80 mmHg and there are a few bibasal crackles. Which auscultatory finding would best explain his presentation?
set.explanation: Exertional syncope, angina and breathlessness in an older patient with a narrow pulse pressure (110/80 mmHg) form the classic triad of severe aortic stenosis, whose murmur is a harsh crescendo–decrescendo (ejection) systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the carotids, often with a soft A2 and a slow-rising pulse. Once symptoms develop, survival without valve replacement is only a few years (shortest with heart failure), so urgent echocardiography and referral for AVR or TAVI follow. An early diastolic murmur indicates AR, an apical holosystolic murmur MR, a midsystolic click MVP and a rub pericarditis.

set.stem: A 72-year-old man has intermittent breathlessness on exertion, palpitations and a cough occasionally productive of blood. On auscultation, a low-pitched diastolic rumbling murmur is faintly heard at the apex. What is the most likely cause of the murmur?
set.explanation: Exertional breathlessness, palpitations (often AF) and haemoptysis with a low-pitched apical diastolic rumble describe mitral stenosis, which is most often a late consequence of rheumatic fever in childhood or youth, typically presenting decades later. Long-standing hypertension causes an S4 and LVH, a silent MI can cause MR (a systolic murmur), congenital mitral stenosis is rare and presents in childhood, and anaemia causes systolic flow murmurs. In older patients, degenerative mitral annular calcification is an increasingly common non-rheumatic cause.

set.stem: A 68-year-old man is intubated in the emergency department because of pulmonary oedema. His BP is 150/90 mmHg. Urgent echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 45% and severe mitral regurgitation. Despite aggressive diuresis with furosemide, he still requires mechanical ventilation for pulmonary oedema. What is the best next step?
options: Start IV afterload reduction (e.g. nitroprusside or IV enalaprilat)
set.explanation: In severe MR, afterload reduction lowers systemic vascular resistance so that more of the LV stroke volume goes forward into the aorta instead of back into the left atrium, reducing the regurgitant fraction and pulmonary venous pressure. With an adequate BP, an IV vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside, nitrates or an IV ACE inhibitor) is the next step after diuretics; an intra-aortic balloon pump is used when the patient is hypotensive. Mitral valve repair or replacement is the definitive treatment once he is stabilised (urgently in acute MR such as papillary muscle rupture), whereas a beta-blocker acutely depresses contractility and a second loop diuretic will not correct the haemodynamic problem.

why: Added BP 150/90 mmHg so that vasodilator therapy (rather than an IABP for hypotension) is the single best answer; option broadened from IV enalapril to IV afterload reduction

set.stem: A nurse at a community clinic has listed patients scheduled for a dental extraction who may need antibiotic prophylaxis. Which of these patients is most likely to benefit from antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis?
options: 17-year-old boy with coarctation of the aorta
26-year-old woman with a ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood
65-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve
set.explanation: AHA and ESC guidelines limit antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures involving the gingiva or root canal to the highest-risk patients: prosthetic valves (including transcatheter valves and repairs using prosthetic material), previous infective endocarditis, and unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease or congenital repairs with prosthetic material within 6 months or with residual defects. A single dose of amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes beforehand is used. Coarctation, a VSD repaired in childhood without residual defect, mitral valve prolapse and native aortic stenosis do not qualify; in the UK, NICE does not recommend routine prophylaxis even for high-risk patients.

set.stem: A 62-year-old man who had a mechanical mitral valve replacement 4 years ago is reviewed. Which long-term antithrombotic therapy is he likely to be taking?
set.explanation: Mechanical valves require lifelong warfarin (a vitamin K antagonist), with a target INR of about 2.5–3.5 for a mechanical mitral valve and 2.0–3.0 for a low-thrombogenicity bileaflet aortic valve without additional risk factors. DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves because dabigatran caused more thrombosis and bleeding than warfarin (RE-ALIGN trial), and antiplatelet drugs alone are inadequate. Low-dose aspirin is added only for specific indications such as atherosclerotic disease.

set.stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with fatigue and exertional breathlessness. He has no significant past history, takes no medication, and does not smoke or drink alcohol. He is very tall (2.08 m) and thin, with a high-arched palate. Auscultation reveals a pansystolic murmur that is loudest in inspiration. What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?
set.explanation: A pansystolic murmur that becomes louder on inspiration (Carvallo sign) is right-sided: inspiration increases venous return to the right heart and hence tricuspid regurgitant flow. In Marfan syndrome, TR can result from tricuspid valve prolapse, which often accompanies mitral valve prolapse. Mitral regurgitation and VSD murmurs are pansystolic but do not increase with inspiration (left-sided murmurs are louder in expiration), mitral stenosis gives a diastolic rumble, and pulmonary regurgitation an early diastolic murmur.

set.stem: A 45-year-old woman who injects drugs presents with breathlessness and bilateral leg swelling. Her pulse is regular, there is a pansystolic murmur heard loudest at the lower left sternal edge, and there is shifting dullness in the abdomen. What is the most likely finding in her jugular venous pulse?
set.explanation: In a person who injects drugs, a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge with ascites and leg oedema indicates tricuspid regurgitation, often from right-sided (Staphylococcus aureus) endocarditis. Blood regurgitating into the right atrium during ventricular systole produces giant v (cv) waves in the JVP that obliterate the x descent, with a pulsatile liver. Cannon a waves occur with AV dissociation, prominent a waves with tricuspid stenosis or pulmonary hypertension, a prominent x descent with tamponade, and absent a waves with AF (excluded by her regular pulse).

why: 'Absent x descent' is also a feature of severe TR; replaced with 'absent a waves' (excluded by the regular pulse)

set.stem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with a bisferiens pulse?
set.explanation: A bisferiens (double-peaked) pulse, with two systolic peaks, is typical of mixed aortic valve disease with predominant regurgitation, and also occurs in severe AR and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. Isolated aortic stenosis gives a slow-rising, low-volume pulse, a PDA a collapsing pulse, cardiac tamponade pulsus paradoxus, and severe LV failure pulsus alternans.

set.stem: Which one of the following is a cause of a soft second heart sound?
set.explanation: In severe calcific aortic stenosis the rigid, immobile valve produces a soft or absent aortic component of S2 (and, with prolonged LV ejection, reversed splitting). An atrial septal defect gives wide fixed splitting, mitral stenosis a loud S1 and opening snap with a normal or loud S2, mitral regurgitation a soft S1, and pulmonary hypertension a loud P2.

why: Aortic regurgitation removed as a distractor because a rigid regurgitant aortic valve can also give a soft A2; replaced with atrial septal defect

set.stem: Which of the following conditions is NOT associated with the development of aortic regurgitation?
set.explanation: Aortic regurgitation results from disease of the valve leaflets (rheumatic fever, infective endocarditis, bicuspid valve) or dilatation of the aortic root (Marfan syndrome, ankylosing spondylitis and other seronegative spondyloarthropathies, syphilitic aortitis, hypertension, aortic dissection). Dilated cardiomyopathy dilates the LV and the mitral annulus, causing functional mitral (and tricuspid) regurgitation, but it does not affect the aortic root or valve.

set.stem: A 2-year-old boy is seen by his GP because his parents are concerned that he is struggling to gain weight and is excessively breathless on exertion. He has known congenital pulmonary stenosis, managed conservatively so far, and the parents ask whether intervention may be needed. What murmur is likely to be heard on examination?
set.explanation: Pulmonary stenosis produces an ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge, often with an ejection click and a soft, delayed P2; like other right-sided murmurs it is louder on inspiration, which increases venous return to the right heart. Aortic stenosis gives an ejection systolic murmur louder in expiration, MR a holosystolic murmur louder in expiration, TR a holosystolic murmur louder on inspiration, and MVP a late systolic murmur after a click. Symptomatic or severe pulmonary stenosis is treated with balloon valvuloplasty.
